Newborn green anacondas emerge from the female's body at a surprisingly modest size, with birth occurring after a well-defined gestation interval. Captive observations indicate that embryonic development at a stable temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C] requires approximately 195 days [ab = approximately 195 days], a duration that aligns with the six-to-seven-month gestation reported in field accounts. At the moment of parturition, each fully formed neonate measures roughly 75 centimeters [Lb = roughly 75 centimeters] in total length, though wild-caught newborns documented in the literature vary somewhat, with birth lengths ranging from 38 to 51 centimeters. This initial size is accompanied by a wet weight at birth of 333 grams [Wwb = 333 grams], a value obtained from a captive-born specimen studied by Abuy et al. in 2003. The relatively low mass relative to length reflects the streamlined, muscular morphology that characterizes this species from its very first day of independent existence, an adaptation that likely facilitates early aquatic locomotion and concealment among submerged vegetation.

Growth during the juvenile stage is remarkably rapid for a serpent of such large ultimate dimensions, though the trajectory toward maturity unfolds over several years. Female green anacondas typically attain reproductive maturity at a total length of 302 centimeters [Lp = 302 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 15000 grams [Wwp = approximately 15000 grams] at puberty. In terms of chronological age, first reproduction under captive conditions held at 29 °C [T = 29 °C] occurs at approximately 1095 days after birth [tR = approximately 1095 days after birth], which is equivalent to roughly three years. This extended juvenile period allows for substantial somatic growth before the energetic demands of gestation and parturition commence. The species is among the heaviest snakes in the world, and the mass gain between birth and reproductive onset is considerable, reflecting a foraging strategy that capitalizes on abundant prey in the seasonally flooded wetlands of South America. Females cease feeding during gestation, making their pre-pregnancy body condition a critical determinant of reproductive success.

The maximum attainable size in this species is prodigious, cementing the green anaconda's reputation as a superlative among modern reptiles. The total length at which somatic growth effectively ceases, known as the ultimate total length, reaches 914 centimeters [Li = 914 centimeters], a value that corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 250000 grams [Wwi = 250000 grams]. Such an enormous mass, approximately 550 pounds, is attained only by the largest females, which exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism compared to the smaller males. To put this in perspective, an individual of this size has a body mass roughly 750 times greater than its 333-gram birth weight (333 grams) [Wwb = 333 grams], an extraordinary multiplier that underscores the species' capacity for sustained hyperphagia and efficient assimilation. This colossal size also influences predation risk, as adult anacondas have few natural enemies beyond humans and perhaps the occasional caiman or jaguar that might target a smaller individual. The ultimate length is rarely achieved in the wild, as most individuals succumb to injury, disease, or intraspecific aggression before reaching asymptotic size.

Longevity in the green anaconda is considerable for a large snake, and captive records provide a useful benchmark for understanding its life-history pace. Under controlled conditions maintained at 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan reaches approximately 10950 days [am = approximately 10950 days], which translates to roughly thirty years. This extended lifespan is consistent with the reproductive schedule of the species, in which females do not reproduce annually; instead, they often skip one or more breeding seasons to replenish body reserves. The maximum reproductive rate, calculated as the product of clutch size and clutch frequency at the same thermal regime of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], indicates that females can produce clutches of 20 to 40 offspring [N_R_i = clutches of 20 to 40 offspring] per reproductive event. Under optimal conditions, a female may produce approximately 3 to 5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 to 5 clutches per year], though biennial breeding is more common in the wild due to the metabolic costs of gestation. The combination of a large clutch size and a relatively low annual frequency yields a moderate lifetime reproductive output, constrained by the trade-off between offspring number and the substantial investment in each large, yolk-rich young.

Ecologically, the green anaconda functions as an apex predator within the aquatic ecosystems of the Orinoco and Amazon basins, where its life-history parameters are finely tuned to the prevailing thermal and hydrological regimes. The stable incubation temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C] that determines the duration of the embryonic phase, measured at 195 days [ab = 195 days], and the onset of first reproduction (1095 days after birth) [tR = 1095 days after birth], reflects the relatively constant temperatures of lowland tropical environments. Nevertheless, seasonal flooding cycles influence prey availability, which in turn affects growth rates and the age at which females reach the 302-centimeter total length at puberty (302 centimeters) [Lp = 302 centimeters]. The substantial wet weight at puberty of 15000 grams [Wwp = 15000 grams] ensures that a female has sufficient energy reserves to sustain a 195-day gestation (approximately 195 days) [ab = approximately 195 days] without feeding at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. Her ultimate mass of 250000 grams [Wwi = 250000 grams] at a body length of 914 centimeters [Li = 914 centimeters] enables her to dominate the aquatic food web, constraining prey populations from capybaras to caimans. This combination of a moderate lifespan of 10950 days [am = 10950 days], a delayed reproductive onset, and a low annual clutch frequency is characteristic of a slow life-history strategy, in which individual survival and the production of high-quality offspring are prioritized over fecundity at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C].
